title: Mamluk Cairo
hook: former slave-soldiers rule Egypt and build mosques, hospitals and schools

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Tusi's observatory on a hilltop at Maragha, paid for by a Mongol prince. Your line was: learning survived. Did you look up, and learn the name of one thing in the sky? Day nine hundred sixty-three.

A boy is sold in a market far from home, somewhere on the grasslands north of the Black Sea. He is shipped to Egypt. There he is taught Arabic, the Qur'an and prayer, and then the horse, the bow and the lance. When his training ends, he is freed, and he becomes a soldier of the sultan. That was the path of the mamluks. Some boys who walked it ended up as sultans themselves, ruling Egypt from the citadel above Cairo. And then they started to build. Today's words: Mamluk Cairo.
screen: `A BOY SOLD FAR FROM HOME.` → `TRAINED, THEN FREED.` → `SOME BECAME SULTANS.`

segments.voice: In Arabic, mamluk means one who is owned. It's worth sitting with that word, because it's honest. These were children bought and taken from their families. Nothing in today's story makes that good. What the story shows is what some of them did once they held power. They built. Walk down the old main street of Cairo today and their buildings are still standing shoulder to shoulder: mosques, schools, fountains, tombs. Sultan Qalawun, who began as a mamluk himself, built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital, a bimaristan, side by side. The endowment that paid for the hospital, as historians describe it, was meant for anyone who was sick, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge. Later, Qalawun's grandson Sultan Hasan, born a prince rather than bought, built a great mosque and college, with space for teaching the different schools of Sunni law under one roof. Why build like this? Partly for memory and standing, like rulers anywhere. But there's a teaching underneath it, one taught in the very schools they built. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that when a person dies, their deeds come to an end, except three: a charity that keeps on giving, knowledge that others benefit from, and a righteous child who prays for them. A hospital is a charity that keeps on giving. A school is knowledge that keeps being used. Men who had once been owned, and their heirs, may well have been thinking about what they would leave behind when they owned nothing again. Hence the line: slaves became builders. The stones are still there. People still pray in some of those mosques.
screen: `MAMLUK — ONE WHO IS OWNED.` · `QALAWUN: A TOMB, A SCHOOL, A HOSPITAL.` · `SULTAN HASAN'S MOSQUE AND COLLEGE.` · `THREE DEEDS THAT DON'T END.` · then, large: `SLAVES BECAME BUILDERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to visit an old building near you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the oldest building you can get to this week: a mosque, a church, a library, a town hall, a school, a bridge. Picture yourself at its door. Look for the details a hurried visitor misses: a step worn hollow by feet, a carved date or a name over the entrance, a patch where the stone has been mended. What was it built to do, and what does it do now? If you pray, you can ask that whatever good it still does keep going. If you don't, simply choose the day you'll go. The bell holds the time.
Mamluk Cairo. The city ruled by former slave-soldiers, who filled it with mosques, schools and hospitals that still stand. Today's words.
Your line: slaves became builders. This week, step inside one old building near you, look up at the ceiling for a moment, and find out one thing about who built it. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of sadaqah jariyah, ongoing charity, and some give to build or keep up mosques, schools, wells and hospitals in the hope that the good continues after them.

fork.setup: you're Qalawun. you were bought as a boy, and now you're sultan of Egypt, with wealth to spend and a name to leave. what do you build?
options: a palace for yourself and your heirs.
a tomb with a school and a hospital beside it.
nothing. you put it all into the army.
fork.reveal: he built a complex with his tomb, a school and a hospital side by side, a charity that keeps on giving.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mamluks were slave soldiers, and that's all.
what it means: boys bought and trained, then freed, who came to rule Egypt and filled Cairo with mosques, schools and hospitals.
what a scholar hears: Qalawun's complex and its bimaristan endowment, Sultan Hasan's college, and the hadith of the three deeds in Sahih Muslim.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1631 (when a person dies, their deeds end except three)
The complex of Sultan Qalawun and its endowment deed; the mosque-madrasa of Sultan Hasan (standard histories of Mamluk Cairo)

notes: No dates, numbers of buildings or patients given, under the claims rule.
The mamluk path (boys bought, often from the Kipchak steppe north of the Black Sea, trained, then manumitted) is standard history but generalized; confirm wording.
Qalawun's bimaristan endowment being for all sick people, rich or poor, man or woman, without charge, is attributed to 'historians'; confirm.
Sultan Hasan's complex as housing teaching in the four Sunni schools of law ('the different schools'); confirm.
'Their buildings are still standing shoulder to shoulder' on Cairo's old main street (al-Mu'izz Street) and 'people still pray in some of those mosques': confirm.

Editor: the practice's 'who paid for it, who swept its floors, thank them in your head' repeated day 949, so it now prepares the visit by looking for concrete details; softened a line stating what the mamluks were thinking; varied the stock 'That's today's line'.
Audit (y3 957-966): Sultan Hasan was Qalawun's grandson, born a prince and never a mamluk himself; the teach now says so, and 'men who had once been owned' now adds 'and their heirs'.
